Here are the Git commands you'll use 90% of the time, grouped by where they fit in your daily workflow.

# Initial setup

```text
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```
Set your identity once. It gets attached to every commit you make.

# Start / clone a repo

```text
git init                  # turn current folder into a repo
git clone <url>           # download an existing repo
```

# Check status (run this constantly)

```text
git status                # what's modified, staged, or untracked
git diff                  # unstaged changes vs last commit
git diff --staged         # staged changes vs last commit
```

# Stage & commit

```text
git add <file>            # stage a specific file
git add .                 # stage all changes in current dir
git commit -m "message"   # commit staged changes
git commit -am "message"  # stage tracked files AND commit in one step
git commit --amend        # fix the last commit message
```
> Running `git commit -m "..."` avoids the Vim editor issue you hit earlier — you supply the message directly on the command line.

# Branches

```text
git branch                # list branches
git branch <name>         # create a branch
git checkout <name>       # switch to a branch
git switch <name>         # modern alternative to checkout
git checkout -b <name>    # create + switch in one go
git merge <branch>        # merge a branch into current one
git branch -d <name>      # delete a branch
```

# Sync with remote

```text
git remote add origin <url>   # link local repo to a remote
git remote -v                 # list remotes
git fetch                     # download changes (no merge)
git pull                      # fetch + merge
git push                      # upload your commits
git push -u origin <branch>   # push and set upstream
```

# History & inspection

```text
git log                  # full commit history
git log --oneline        # condensed, one line per commit
git log --graph          # text-based branch graph
git show <SHA>           # details of a specific commit
git blame <file>         # who changed each line and when
```

# Undo / fix mistakes

```text
git restore <file>              # discard local changes to a file
git reset HEAD <file>           # unstage a file, keep changes
git reset --soft HEAD~1         # undo last commit, keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1         # undo last commit, DISCARD changes
git revert <SHA>                # new commit that undoes a past commit (safe for shared branches)
```

# Temporary stash (when you need to switch branches mid-work)

```text
git stash          # save uncommitted changes
git stash pop      # bring them back
```

---

**The daily loop you'll repeat most:**

```text
git status → git add . → git commit -m "msg" → git push
```

That's really the heart of it. Everything else (rebase, reflog, cherry-pick, etc.) comes up occasionally, but you can go a long way with just the commands above.

# Switch from HTTPS to SSH

If your repo is:

```
https://github.com/yourname/myproject.git
```

Then the SSH equivalent is:

```
git@github.com:yourname/myproject.git
```

Check current GIT 

```
git remote -v
```

If not SSH, then use below code to switch

```
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPO.git
```
